Rachmad, Yoesoep Edhie. 2022. Psychological Innovation Theory. Hoorn Gouden Eeuw Boek Internationale Uitgeverij, Speciale Editie 2022. https://doi.org/10.17605/osf.io/2sq7x Psychological Innovation Theory, introduced by Yoesoep Edhie Rachmad in 2022, emerged from the need to understand how innovation can be driven through psychological approaches. In a constantly changing and challenging world, innovation is key to organizational success and sustainability. This theory was developed to provide guidance on how individuals and organizations can create environments that foster creativity and innovation through the understanding and management of psychological factors. Definition and Basic Concepts Psychological Innovation Theory defines psychological innovation as the process by which individuals and groups use psychological insights to create new ideas and effective solutions. The basic concept of this theory is that understanding motivation, emotions, and cognition can be used to drive creativity and find new approaches to problems. The theory emphasizes the importance of internal factors such as self-confidence, intrinsic motivation, and openness to new experiences in fostering innovation. Underlying Phenomena The theory is based on the phenomenon that many organizations face barriers to fostering innovation due to a lack of understanding of the psychological factors underlying creativity. For example, fear of failure, lack of emotional support, and a culture that does not support risk-taking can hinder innovation. This phenomenon shows that innovation relies not only on technical skills but also on the ability to create a psychologically supportive environment. When individuals feel safe to experiment and share ideas, they are more likely to produce innovative solutions. Working Principles The working principles of Psychological Innovation Theory involve several key steps. First, it is important to create a supportive psychological environment where individuals feel safe to take risks and experiment. Second, providing emotional support and motivation is crucial to encourage engagement and creativity. Third, developing openness to new experiences and different perspectives is essential. The theory also emphasizes the importance of self-reflection and learning from failure as part of the innovation process. Indicators Key indicators of this theory include the level of individual and team creativity, the number of new ideas generated, and the success of innovation implementation. Other indicators include the level of openness to new experiences, intrinsic motivation, and job satisfaction. These indicators can be measured through surveys, interviews, and analysis of work outcomes in various contexts. They help evaluate how well individuals and organizations succeed in fostering innovation through psychological approaches. Operational Variables Operational variables of Psychological Innovation Theory include measuring levels of creativity, quality of emotional support, and openness to new experiences. These variables can be measured through surveys, self-assessments, and performance data analysis. This data provides insights into how psychological factors influence the innovation process and how interventions can be designed to enhance creativity and innovation. Application Areas The theory can be applied in various fields such as Human Resource Management (HRM), Psychology, Education, Social Communication, and Health. In HRM, the theory helps develop programs that increase employee creativity and innovation. In Psychology, it is useful for understanding how psychological factors can be used to drive innovation. In Education, the theory supports the development of curricula that promote creativity and innovative thinking among students. In Social Communication, the theory guides strategies to enhance engagement and innovation within communities. In Health, the theory helps design programs that support innovation in care and health management. Determining Factors The success of applying this theory is determined by several key factors. Support from leaders and management is crucial for creating an environment that supports innovation. Additionally, adequate training and resources to develop creative skills are essential. Success also depends on the ability to use self-reflection and learning from failure as part of the innovation process. Implementation and Strategies Implementing this theory requires a structured and ongoing approach. The first step is identifying the needs and barriers to innovation within the organization and developing appropriate programs. Effective strategies include providing training on creativity and innovation, developing policies that support experimentation and risk-taking, and creating mechanisms for feedback and evaluation. Continuous evaluation and adjustment of strategies based on feedback from individuals are critical for ensuring long-term success. Supporting and Hindering Challenges Challenges in applying this theory include resistance to change, lack of understanding of the importance of psychological factors in innovation, and limited resources to develop and implement innovation programs. However, with strong support from leaders and a supportive organizational culture, along with ongoing education, these challenges can be overcome. Success also relies on the ability to create an environment that fosters individual engagement and innovation, as well as the ability to manage conflicts and barriers that may arise in the innovation process. Conclusion Psychological Innovation Theory emphasizes the importance of psychological factors in driving creativity and innovation. The theory provides a comprehensive framework for understanding and facilitating the innovation process across various fields. With proper application, this theory can help individuals and organizations enhance their ability to innovate, better face challenges, and create a positive impact on performance and well-being. In the contemporary digital landscape, cybersecurity transcends mere technological challenges, intertwining intricately with human behavior and cognition. This review delves into the vital intersection of psychology and cybersecurity, aiming to unveil the multifaceted human dimensions of digital resilience. By delving into the nuances of human decision-making, biases, and responses to cyber perils, one can bolster defensive mechanisms and augment resilience against dynamic digital threats. Employing a multidisciplinary approach drawing from psychology, behavioral economics, and cybersecurity expertise, this study sheds light on various aspects. These include the pivotal role of human factors in security, the sophisticated manipulation tactics employed in social engineering, the indispensable nature of user-centric design, and the profound psychological impact of cyber threats on individuals and organizations alike. Furthermore, this facilitates the creation of resilient digital ecosystems capable of withstanding the ever-evolving landscape of cyber threats. This comprehensive study understanding fosters the enhancement of cybersecurity measures, ensuring the protection of individuals, organizations, and critical digital infrastructure.

This quantitative study employs a descriptive-correlation research design to determine the motivation and pedagogical competence level of public elementary teachers teaching non-readers in a school district in Alamada, Cotabato, Philippines. It further examined the influence of their motivation on their pedagogical competence. Thirty-five teachers from Grades 1-3 participated in the study. More so, the study utilized content-validated and pilot-tested survey questionnaires to extract the data from the respondents. Descriptive statistics, such as frequency count, mean, and percentage, were utilized, and multiple linear regression was employed for the correlation test. Based on the result, the teachers' overall level of motivation to teach non-readers was very high. More so, the responses indicated a high level of identified regulation, reflecting strong intrinsic motivation. Both introjected regulation and extrinsic motivation were also reported as high, while amotivation was notably low. Moreover, the data revealed that the teachers in Grades 1-3 from one school district in said town were considered very competent. However, this present study found that there is no significant influence between teachers’ motivation and their pedagogical competence in teaching non-readers. The current study recommends that school administrators consider possible actions directed towards sustaining and enhancing high motivation because it can still impact teaching effectiveness and student outcomes while teaching non-readers.

documents.abstract: Public servants’ intrinsic motivation—‘their experience of enjoyment, interest and satisfaction in work’—is an important correlate of performance (Wright 2004; Cerasoli et al. 2014; Sansone & Harackiewicz 2000) and well-being (Ryan & Deci 2000). Conversely, a lack of intrinsic motivation inhibits the creativity (Houtgraaf & Ropes in press; Houtgraaf et al. 2021; Houtgraaf et al. 2023) and productivity (Grant 2008; Becchetti et al. 2013) required to provide the effective, user-centered policies/services that citizens need and demand (Clarke et al. 2007; Van Thiel 2017; Torfing 2016). Furthermore, inadequate motivation diminishes public servants’ experienced wellbeing (Barret-Cheetham et al. 2016; Borst 2018) and is associated with dissatisfaction, boreout, burnout, turnover and part-time work in the public sector (Kim 2018; Borst & Knies 2023; Stazyk et al. 2011). Adequate levels of intrinsic motivation are thus of central importance for both workforce performance, well-being and retention. Meanwhile, both practitioners and academics voice that captivating and retaining public servants is increasingly becoming a challenge—especially with more junior public servants. In general, attracting and retaining an intrinsically motivated workforce appears difficult due to numerous developments in both the nature of work and the nature of employees (Davidesque et al. 2020; Twenge et al. 2010; Cahill et al. 2012). In the public sector too, sustainable employment is of growing concern, illustrated by efforts to understand and safeguard public servants’ well-being, performance and retention (Van der Meer et al. 2022; Borst & Knies 2023; Johari et al. 2019). The challenges of captivating and retaining seems especially true for employees from more recent generations—or at least of younger age (Schröder 2023)—that are argued to have different and more pronounced expectations and preferences relating to work (Waworuntu et al. 2022). In the Netherlands, for example, the translated ‘captivate and bind’ programs sprout throughout the public sector in an alarmed effort to retain (junior) public servants (Binnenlands Bestuur 2024). However, our knowledge regarding intrinsic motivation amidst bureaucratic constraints falls short on two major accounts. Firstly, insight is lacking on whether a lack of intrinsic motivation is an issue in the public sector as a result of bureaucratic constraints and through what mechanisms this would or would not occur. On the one hand, bureaucratic constraints such as formalization and centralization arguably have several negative effects that relate to a lack of intrinsic motivation (Giauque et al. 2012; George et al. 2021; Lavigna 2013; Serhan et al. 2018). On the other hand, such bureaucratic constraints might not lead to amotivation as public servants’ motivation is argued to be a relatively stable concept (Baldwin 1990; Houtgraaf & Ropes in press) and because public servants’ argued idiosyncratic personality may actually lead them to value bureaucratic elements (Leisha & DeHart-Davis 2007; Merton 1940; Bozeman & Rainey 1998). Applying Self-Determination Theory and assessing whether bureaucratic constraints as forms of external locus of control diminish public servants’ sense of autonomy and competence and thereby lead to amotivation (Ryan & Deci 2000, see also Ekval 1996) would provide insight on underlying mechanisms but has not been applied. Secondly, insight is lacking on the role of age/generation, despite evidence pointing towards a significant moderating function. Millennials and more recent generations are argued to assign particular value to elements of autonomy and positive hierarchical feedback relating to competence in their work (Waworuntu et al. 2022), which appears at odds with bureaucratic constraints such as formalization and centralization typically present in the public sector that may stifle such senses of autonomy and competence (Boyne 2002; Bozeman 2000; Ekval 1996). Moreover, recent findings dispute that such differences relating to work motivation and preferences are a result of generational differences but a function of age (Schröder 2023). In short, insight is lacking on whether and why bureaucratic constraints relate to amotivation, what role age/generation plays and thus what strategies and tactics to employ in order to captivate and retain public servants—especially junior ones. Therefore, the goal of this study was to scrutinize whether and how bureaucratic dimensions relate to public servants’ intrinsic motivation whilst paying particular attention to self-determination as an underlying mechanism and the role of age. To these ends, several analyses are conducted on cross-sectional data from 1158 public servants working in a range of Dutch public sector organizations to answer the research question: ‘Through which mechanisms do levels of public servants’ intrinsic motivation correlate with the presence of bureaucratic dimensions, taking into account age?’. Scrutinizing these mechanisms allowed for detailed insights in mechanisms of intrinsic motivation and how to safeguard it in the public sector context, especially among specific age groups. The ensuing results provide public sector practitioners, managers, HR-departments and training organizations with avenues on whether and how to effectively counter adverse effects of bureaucratic dimensions on public servants’ motivation in order to captivate and retain public servants’ and in turn improve their performance, wellbeing and sustainable employment. MOTIVATION AMIDST BUREAUCRATIC CONSTRAINTS Intrinsic motivation and Self-Determination Theory Intrinsic motivation encompasses an experience of enjoyment, interest and satisfaction in work that stems from the employee itself, instead of external factors (Wright 2004; Ryan & Deci 2000; Li et al. 2015). According to Self-Determination Theory, the central characteristic of intrinsic motivation is that it stems from an internal locus of control whereby the individual experiences a control over its own actions and outcomes, instead of an external locus of control whereby the individual experiences that its actions and outcomes are determined by external factors such as managers or rules (Deci & Ryan 1985; Li et al. 2015). In more detail, according to Self-Determination Theory, senses of autonomy, competence and relatedness are essential psychological needs that can be satisfied or frustrated and thus determine the degree of an internal locus of control and experience of intrinsic motivation: the individual has to perceive itself as an autonomous actor that is able and capable of acting in correspondence with its values and goals (Chen et al. 2015; Deci & Ryan 1985). External locus of control, however, may lead to a lack of perceived internal locus of control, hampering intrinsic motivation (Bénabou & Tirole 2003; Deci and Ryan 1985) and leading to amotivation whereby the enjoyment, interest and satisfaction of work becomes increasingly absent (Howard et al., 2016). In general, intrinsic motivation is perceived as beneficial for performance and well-being (Houtgraaf & Ropes in press; Ryan & Deci 2000; Grant 2008; Becchetti et al. 2013), which results in the reasoning that an impairing external locus of control that may hamper employees’ intrinsic motivation ought to be avoided. When assessing intrinsic motivation, it is important to determine whether the concept is approached as an attitude or a state, depending on the goal and timeline of assessment. If considered an attitude, intrinsic motivation is assessed based on an individual’s recall over a longer period of time based on the remembering-self, thereby leading to a more average and stable assessment of the level of intrinsic motivation, whereas if considered a state, intrinsic motivation is assessed on based on an individual’s experience in the current moment based on the experiencing-self, thereby leading to accurate but momentarily and fluctuating assessments of levels of intrinsic motivation (Kahneman & Riis 2005). As the goal of this study concerns assessing how individuals recall their work contexts and attitudes in general and on average in order to assess relations, intrinsic motivation is approached and measured as an attitude in this study (Lee & Choi 2003). Formalization as external locus of control Formalization—the degree to which work related processes and interactions are generally governed by formal rules, standard policies and procedures (Boyne 2002; Bozeman 2000)—can be perceived as representing external locus of control that may hamper public servants’ intrinsic motivation. Formalization is a typical bureaucratic dimension of mechanistic organizations (Brown 2014) and although public sector reforms have aimed at reduction of formalization (Van Thiel 2001), public sector organizations are characterized as featuring at least certain levels of formalization (Borins 2010; Boyne 2002; Boye et al. 2022; Houtgraaf et al. 2023). The object of such bureaucratic principles as expressed in formalization is to achieve stability, standardization and to avoid flexibility and change (Ekval 1996) by controlling employee behavior (Hirst et al. 2009). As such, formalization is a clear example of external locus of control that may hamper intrinsic motivation. Arguably, the underlying mechanisms are twofold. On the one hand, the rules and procedures imposed by formalization may frustrate a sense of autonomy as the individual might not be able to act as it would without these external controls (Hirst et al. 2009). On the other hand, formalization its rules and procedures are related to passive, rule-bound and anxious behavior to stay inside established boundaries (Ekval 1996), which may frustrate a sense of competence as the individual might feel less capable and efficacious in conducting work as a result of the external controls (Au 2015). INTRODUCTION: We present the first case of pediatric ileocystoplasty using a purely robotic approach in Spain. CASE REPORT: 12-year-old male with neurogenic bladder of low capacity and high pressures. After failure of conservative treatment, bladder augmentation with ileum patch was decided upon. Surgery was carried out using a purely robotic approach with 4 robotic and 2 accessory ports. Surgery duration was 380 minutes in total, without intraoperative complications. He was discharged 2 weeks after cystographic control. During 32-months follow-up, he has remained continent. DISCUSSION: The minimal invasion, surgical precision and ergonomics made the robotic approach an optimal option for complex surgical techniques. Given the little availability of the robot and the low pediatric volume, its standardization is a challenge. Our accumulated experience is consistent with the current literature and shows promising surgical and esthetic results. We hope this case report will contribute to the divulgation and progressive introduction of robotic surgery in our daily lives.

BACKGROUND: Employee Occupational Health ('occupational health') clinicians have expansive perspectives of the experience of healthcare personnel. Integrating mental health into the purview of occupational health is a newer approach that could combat historical limitations of healthcare personnel mental health programmes, which have been isolated and underused. OBJECTIVE: We aimed to document innovation and opportunities for supporting healthcare personnel mental health through occupational health clinicians. This work was part of a national qualitative needs assessment of employee occupational health clinicians during COVID-19 who were very much at the centre of organisational responses. DESIGN: This qualitative needs assessment included key informant interviews obtained using snowball sampling methods. PARTICIPANTS: We interviewed 43 US Veterans Health Administration occupational health clinicians from 29 facilities. APPROACH: This analysis focused on personnel mental health needs and opportunities, using consensus coding of interview transcripts and modified member checking. KEY RESULTS: Three major opportunities to support mental health through occupational health involved: (1) expanded mental health needs of healthcare personnel, including opportunities to support work-related concerns (eg, traumatic deployments), home-based concerns and bereavement (eg, working with chaplains); (2) leveraging expanded roles and protocols to address healthcare personnel mental health concerns, including opportunities in expanding occupational health roles, cross-disciplinary partnerships (eg, with employee assistance programmes (EAP)) and process/protocol (eg, acute suicidal ideation pathways) and (3) need for supporting occupational health clinicians' own mental health, including opportunities to address overwork/burn-out with adequate staffing/resources. CONCLUSIONS: Occupational health can enact strategies to support personnel mental health: to structurally sustain attention, use social cognition tools (eg, suicidality protocols or expanded job descriptions); to leverage distributed attention, enhance interdisciplinary collaboration (eg, chaplains for bereavement support or EAP) and to equip systems with resources and allow for flexibility during crises, including increased staffing.

Abstract Geoparks are both the concentration of valuable geological remains and an important carrier of tourism activities. Relying on a geographic information system (GIS), this project takes the landscape change of a geopark from 2005 to 2020 as an example, and after processing the remote sensing images, quantitative analysis is carried out by using the landscape pattern index method, which reveals the landscape change characteristics of the sample geopark. The data related to natural and human factors was collected, and the driving factors of landscape changes in geoparks were analyzed by combining probes. The main landscape types of the sample geoparks are cropland, woodland, and rocky desertification land, and the study period presents landscape changes of decreasing cropland area (22.96%), fluctuating woodland area, and increasing desertification area (37.40%), and the development of the park landscape changes presents irregularity and complexity. The main drivers of landscape change in geoparks are geological conditions, topography and geomorphology, vegetation, economic development capacity, and ecological environment quality (q value = 0.438~0.521), of which economic development capacity and ecological environment quality play a dominant role in the interaction of factors (0.86).

The increasing automation of work and increasing reliance on autonomous devices and systems calls for re-conceptualizing information system usage. Thinking of IS usage as the hands-on use of computerized devices through interfaces is increasingly inadequate where roles and responsibilities are delegated to IT-enabled devices and systems that may operate autonomously and may not interact directly with users. This paper’s new IS usage theory (ISUT) consists of three axioms and 12 underlying assumptions that apply to IS usage for nontrivial sociotechnical and totally automated work systems. A background section includes the rationale for pursuing a new view of IS usage and basic concepts related to systems, information systems, work system theory (WST) and the ISUT’s boundary conditions. A summary of selected research articles related to IS usage emphasizes how central ideas in those articles diverge from the ISUT’s underlying assumptions and may not suffice for describing increasingly automated work practices. A two-dimensional agent responsibility framework facilitates the application of the ISUT’s system-oriented view of IS usage by combining a spectrum of IS roles and a series of facets of work. Four illustrative real-world examples demonstrate the practical application of the ISUT. The conclusion emphasizes this paper’s motivation, theory creation process, theory presentation and content, and contribution.

Detecting and reading text from natural images is a hard computer vision task that is central to a variety of emerging applications. Related problems like document character recognition have been widely studied by computer vision and machine learning researchers and are virtually solved for practical applications like reading handwritten digits. Reliably recognizing characters in more complex scenes like photographs, however, is far more difficult: the best existing methods lag well behind human performance on the same tasks. In this paper we attack the problem of recognizing digits in a real application using unsupervised feature learning methods: reading house numbers from street level photos. To this end, we introduce a new benchmark dataset for research use containing over 600,000 labeled digits cropped from Street View images. We then demonstrate the difficulty of recognizing these digits when the problem is approached with hand-designed features. Finally, we employ variants of two recently proposed unsupervised feature learning methods and find that they are convincingly superior on our benchmarks. 1

documents.abstract: Background: Critical View of Safety (CVS) is the accepted strategy to avoid bile duct injury during Laparoscopic Cholecystectomy (LC). In this study, we sought to investigate the accuracy and performance of a trained Artificial Intelligent (AI) model in validation of the CVS achievement during elective LC in a real time operating room setting.Study Design: A deep learning neural network which was previously trained on annotated segments of 700 LC videos to identify the CVS criteria, was integrated into the operating room laparoscopic video system, for continuous monitoring and real-time validation of CVS achievement during elective LC procedures. The system's feedback and surgeon's report were recorded and compared, as well as the overall rate of CVS achievement.Results: Of 40 consecutive LC, CVS was reported by the surgeons in 34 (85%). In all the 6 cases where CVS was not achieved due to severe inflammation or anatomy distortion, the AI model agreed with surgeon's report and did not identify CVS. Out of the 34 cases where CVS was achieved, the AI model identified 33. Thus, the AI model detected the CVS achievement with a specificity of 100% [95%-CI 98.1%, 100%] and sensitivity of 97% [95%-CI 96.1%, 98.2%].Conclusions: A trained AI model can identify CVS during elective LC with very high accuracy in a real time OR setting. Additionally, its use may result in high rates of CVS achievement, thereby improving LC procedure's safety and outcome.

documents.abstract: Gravity and gravity gradient data are widely used in geodesy, geodynamics, oil and mineral exploration, and aided navigation. The measured gravity and gravity gradient data include high-frequency noise caused by instrument system error, environmental conditions, and human factors. Separating noise from the measured gravity and gravity gradient data is one of the most challenging tasks in processing the measured data. Traditional low-pass digital filters can remove the noise of an individual component in real-time, which cannot realize the joint filtering of gravity and gravity gradient data. As a postprocessing method, the inversion-based methods can combine gravity and all the gradient components to remove the noise constrained by the Laplace equation. However, a real-time filter method that combines gravity and all gradient components is needed for some special applications, such as submarine gravity and gravity gradient-aided navigation. In this study, gravity and gravity gradient data are combined in establishing system equation and measurement equation of the standard Kalman filter, and denoised in real-time by the improved Kalman filter (IKF). Based on the model test, this method can simultaneously remove the noise in gravity and gravity gradient data in real-time, and ensure denoising performance. Finally, we apply this method to real gravity and gravity gradient data in St. George’s Bay, Canada, acquired by Bell Geospace, and compared the denoised results by full tensor noise reduction (FTNR) and Gaussian low-pass filter, which verified that the performance of IKF is well in real-time joint filtering of gravity and gravity gradient data.
